description: Soy estudiante de Computación e Informática en la Universidad Católica de Trujillo, Perú. Me interesan la programación, el desarrollo de videojuegos y la exploración espacial. Busco crear un juego donde el jugador planifique y ejecute su propia misión espacial. Me gustaría sumar personas con habilidades en programación, diseño gráfico, narración de historias y desarrollo web. ¡Únete si quieres aprender y crear algo increíble!
summary:
Mission Architect is a free, open-source, bilingual (English/Spanish) browser game that lets participants design, manage and simulate a complete space mission — from mission concept to operations.

Players choose one of five real-world-inspired scenarios (lunar cargo resupply, a Mars orbiter, an asteroid-deflection demo, an Earth climate observatory and a deep-space telescope at Sun–Earth L2), then design the spacecraft (structure, power, battery, communications, flight computer, attitude control and propulsion), select from 14 scientific instruments, pick an orbit and a launch vehicle, and pass a NASA-style design review. They then fly an animated simulation with random anomalies — solar flares, reaction-wheel failures, micrometeorite strikes, budget cuts — and receive a scored post-mission report that explains exactly why the mission succeeded or failed.

The game makes the coupled trade-offs of real systems engineering tangible: every instrument adds mass, power, cost and data; every orbit demands ΔV and shapes communications; every rocket limits how much you can launch. It supports solo play and cooperative play for up to four participants with distinct roles, and it teaches the concepts through plain-language feedback, a glossary and links to real NASA resources.
details:
WHAT IT IS
Mission Architect is an interactive, educational space-mission design game built with plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript — no frameworks, no build step, no external services. It runs offline in any modern browser and is fully bilingual (English/Spanish).

WHAT IT DOES
1. Mission briefing — five scenarios inspired by real NASA missions, each with a destination, budget, science goals and mission objectives.
2. Spacecraft design — seven subsystems (structure, power, battery, communications, flight computer, attitude control, propulsion) with 3–4 realistic options each; 14 scientific instruments with distinct mass, power, cost, data and science characteristics.
3. Orbit & launch — ten orbits (LEO to Sun–Earth L2 and an asteroid intercept) with real ΔV, communication-window, coverage and radiation properties, plus five launch vehicles with different capacity, cost and reliability. The game verifies that the rocket can actually lift your spacecraft to your orbit.
4. Design review — a NASA-style checklist (mass, power, battery, budget, data, ΔV, orbit compatibility, science fit, cargo) with PASS / WARN / FAIL feedback that teaches the trade-offs.
5. Mission simulation — animated launch, transit, orbit insertion and operations, with a daily resource model (power vs. eclipse, battery, data backlog vs. onboard storage, radiation damage, science accumulation) and 14 random anomalies that force decisions under pressure.
6. Post-mission report — a 0–100 score with S/A/B/C/D grades across science return, resource efficiency, reliability, objectives met and collaboration, plus a plain-language systems-engineering analysis of what worked and what failed.
7. Modes — solo play, and cooperative play for up to four participants with roles (Mission Director, Systems Engineer, Science Lead, Comms & Resources Manager) and a design-review approval board. A local leaderboard rewards iteration.

HOW IT WORKS (engineering model)
• Mass: bus + payload + cargo + propellant. Propellant mass follows the real rocket equation, m = m_dry · (e^(ΔV / (Isp·g0)) − 1), with a 25% margin.
• Power: solar arrays scale with solar irradiance at the destination (Mars ≈ 43% of Earth); RTGs work anywhere but are heavy and costly. Battery capacity must cover eclipse loads.
• Communications: data downlink = data rate × communication window × 86400 s, with storage limits and backlog losses.
• ΔV: required by the orbit; available from the propulsion system's specific impulse. Events can consume extra propellant.
• Scoring: normalized science return vs. an ideal payload, plus mass/power/budget/data margins, launch-vehicle reliability, health, objectives and collaboration.

BENEFITS
• Turns abstract systems-engineering trade-offs into decisions students can feel and iterate on.
• Accessible to beginners (guided Cadet mode, plain-language feedback) and deep enough for engineering students (Veteran mode, coupled resource model).
• Supports teamwork and negotiation, mirroring how real mission design boards work.
• Free, open source and bilingual — usable in classrooms, clubs and outreach events worldwide.

TOOLS USED
HTML5, CSS3, vanilla JavaScript (ES2020), Canvas 2D. No external libraries, fonts or CDNs. Tested with Node.js (engine) and jsdom (UI smoke tests).
